newsitem.title: USA: Jones sodas -- Soft drinks as fashion statements.
newsitem.headline: Jones sodas -- Soft drinks as fashion statements.

text.p: Forget bottled iced teas, man. They're yesterday. What kind of image does iced tea portray? Borr-ring.
Now take a phosphorescent red or green soft drink. You get the image of snowboarding, tattooing and body piercing, right? The makers of Jones Sodas sure hope so.
"Beverages are a fashion item," said Peter van Stolk, the highly enthusiastic, 30-something president of Jones' parent company, Urban Juice and Soda Co.

Like the right pants, shoes, hair cut or disaffected snarl, you need the right soft drink or bottled water, especially if you're in Generation 2000 -- between the ages of 15 and 35, van Stolk said during a New York visit.

"We think of ourselves as a fashion company," he said of the Vancouver, British Columbia-based bottler and drink distributor. As such, Urban Juice and Soda is not only selling beverages, but is selling a sense of "cool -- by association."

Urban started in 1987 as a soft drink and juice distributor. It has moved into creating its own soft drinks and bottled water, which now makes up about three-quarters of the business. Its stock is traded on the Vancouver Stock Exchange.

The goal is not to compete with the Cokes and Pepsis of the world, but to take a large bite out of the $52 billion "New Age" drinks market -- the segment created by Snapple. But Jones hopes to differ from Snapple, which has oversaturated the market and is suffering from falling sales.

Van Stolk has clearly and methodically plotted Jones' path, and, like any fashion item, expects it to have a five- to seven-year run. Today, Jones sodas and Wazu bottled waters make up 72 percent of Urban's $2.65 million in sales. But before the Jones/Wazu wave crests and falls, Urban will begin another brand to catch the imagination of Generation 2000ers, like another wave in the ocean.
Right now, that product has the code name Blue Dog (there are corporate spies everwhere). "You have to position yourself as the next thing," van Stolk said.
Today's fashion item, Jones, comes in 10 flavors such as lemon-lime, grape, orange and fufu berry in bright electric colours.
"Color is very important to the brand," van Stolk said. The soft drinks come in long-necked bottles, the same ones used to bottle Corona beer.

But what is really going to sell the product, make it a fashion statement, he said, is the label. There are dozens of Generation 2000-inspired paper label photographs, such as Freddy the dog, a woman's legs, bare navels, goteed chins or cityscapes, which can be collected. For a fee, consumers can send in their own photograph to be printed on a limited run label.
With mottos like "I've got a Jones for Jones," or "Wet Yourself," for Wazu water, which comes with its own highly stylised label, Urban's products won't be in every corner grocery.

The company is deliberately targeting accounts in hair salons, tatoo parlours, music stores and snowboard shops. Urban also recently named the world's No. 1 ranked skateboarder, Tony Hawk, and the leading snowboarder, Tom Burt, as athlete endorsers.
With only 22 employees, Urban goes to its public for feedback on flavors. Recently, school children in California were asked to sample some of the Jones flavors and give feedback.
One of the winners was blue bubblegum.

Urban plans to distribute Jones and Wazu drinks to major trend-setting areas such as New York City, California, Toronto and the Pacific Northwest. By March, the products will be distributed to stores in Jones-painted trucks.
The company will advertise on MTV beginning in April, but the most impact will be delivered at the point of sale.

"Color has to punch off the shelves. That's why there are bright colours," said van Stolk, as Urban vice president Jennifer Cue demonstrated a neon light box that will be used as a point-of-sale display.

Image will be furthered by Jones bumper stickers, championed by van Stolk's corporate heroes Ben and Jerry, as well as T-shirts, hats and jackets. There is also a web site, for interested Jonsers (www.jonessoda.com).
There's no time to waste, van Stolk said. Jones only has five to seven years.
